Should I use MBMM? A scientific and practical guide

Source: vignettes/mbmm.Rmd
mbmm.Rmd
library(mbmm)

Start with the scientific question

MBMM is designed for a question of the form:

Does a covariate change the probability of a latent biological state that is expressed through a longitudinal mechanistic trajectory?

The state is not a thresholded measurement. It is a biological condition such as productive infection or a durable antibody gain. The longitudinal record contains evidence about that state, and a mechanistic model says what records from each state should look like.

MBMM separates two tasks:

  1. the trajectory likelihood asks what state is compatible with the participant’s longitudinal measurements; and
  2. the gate asks how a covariate changes the probability of that state.

The primary scientific estimand is the gate coefficient. The trajectory bank is the mechanism used to form state evidence; it is not usually the endpoint of the study.

When MBMM is a good match

MBMM is potentially useful when all of the following are true:

  • the endpoint is a biologically meaningful but unobserved state;
  • state membership changes the shape, scale, timing, or durability of a longitudinal trajectory;
  • a mechanistic model can generate plausible trajectories for that process;
  • repeated measurements contain more information than a single thresholded label;
  • the covariate belongs in the state-probability model, not in the trajectory likelihood used to infer the state;
  • a state-specific kinetic population can be constructed by Route I or Route II; and
  • the bank used to score a participant can be built without that participant’s measurements.

Examples include:

  • whether baseline antibody changes the probability of productive infection, inferred from a complete viral-load trajectory;
  • whether vaccine regimen changes the probability of a durable post-boost gain, inferred from prime-boost antibody kinetics; and
  • whether a treatment changes the probability of entering a mechanistically defined response phenotype rather than merely crossing a visit-specific threshold.

When MBMM is not the right model

Do not use MBMM merely because the data are longitudinal. A different model is usually preferable when:

  • the endpoint is directly observed without meaningful classification error;
  • the scientific target is a continuous kinetic parameter rather than a latent class;
  • there is no defensible mechanistic model or no longitudinal information capable of separating the states;
  • the class boundary was chosen after looking at the same outcomes and cannot be cross-fitted;
  • neither a credible state-specific reference population nor a prespecified identifiable parameter-space region is available;
  • the covariate changes kinetics within a state, violating the gate-only assumption, unless that dependence is explicitly modelled; or
  • the donor kinetic population is not transportable to the analysis cohort.

An honest computation cannot repair a scientifically invalid state definition, a non-transportable reference population, or an inadequate mechanistic model.

Translate the question into MBMM objects

Before writing code, fill in this table for the proposed analysis.

Object Question to answer
Longitudinal data YiY_i Which repeated measurements carry evidence about the state?
Latent state ZiZ_i What biological condition does state 1 mean? What does state 0 mean?
Mechanistic trajectory μ(t;θ)\mu(t; \theta) Which kinetic parameters generate the observed shape?
Covariates xix_i Which variables are hypothesised to shift state probability?
Gate piipi_i What probability is being modelled before using the trajectory evidence?
Kinetic population GkG_k What population of trajectories represents each state?
Class likelihood LikL_{ik} How will trajectory evidence be integrated over that population?
Responsibility wiw_i What participant-level posterior state probability will be reported?

If any row has no scientifically interpretable answer, the analysis is not ready to fit.

Choose Route I or Route II

Route I: known state-specific reference population

Use Route I when a separate donor sample can credibly represent state 1.

Required conditions:

  • Purity: donors represent the intended state, not an unrestricted mixture of states.
  • Transportability: the within-state kinetic distribution applies to the analysis cohort.
  • Honesty: the complete donor-bank construction is independent of the analysis participants.
  • Coverage: the candidate family covers the observed analysis trajectories without relying on implausible boundary candidates.

Continue to the Route I simulation, which builds an independent productive-infection bank with the eclipse-phase viral ODE and checks recovery against known truth.

vignette("pipeline", package = "mbmm")

Route II: prespecified region of kinetic parameter space

Use Route II when no labelled donor sample exists but the scientific state is a region S1S_1 fixed before fitting, such as a positive durable gain.

Required conditions:

  • Target validity: the region corresponds to the scientific state and the boundary is not selected to optimise the observed result.
  • Identifiability: the longitudinal measurements distinguish the relevant kinetic coordinate.
  • Region support: both S1S_1 and its complement carry adequate fitted marginal mass; restriction by nearly zero mass is unstable.
  • Honesty: every outcome-adaptive step, including support screening and weight fitting, excludes the participant being scored.
  • Exchangeability: the remaining participants are a suitable population from which to estimate the held-out participant’s marginal kinetics.

Continue to the Route II simulation, which defines durable gain by g=log10(D1/C1)>0g=log_{10}(D_1/C_1)>0, fits exact leave-one-out marginal banks, and checks recovery against known truth.

vignette("sdy2354", package = "mbmm")

Core package functions, in scientific order

MBMM is not limited to its built-in models. Any positive trajectory function with arguments time and theta can be passed to trajectory_loglik(). The custom ODE walkthrough reconstructs both built-in models from scratch, explains raw parameter boxes and identifiable bank designs, and fits a new HIV constant-beta model.

Scientific step MBMM functions What to verify
Generate mechanistic trajectories eclipse_trajectory(), andraud_trajectory() Curves are biologically plausible over a dense time grid
Construct a candidate family eclipse_design(), user-defined candidate data frames Bounds and screens are fixed independently of scored outcomes
Exclude invalid trajectories screen_positive() Screening rule is mechanistic, or is repeated inside cross-fitting if data-adaptive
Score observations against candidates trajectory_loglik(), obs_loglik() Noise, censoring, visit times, and any timing uncertainty match the data-generating assumptions
Integrate nuisance coordinates pool_marginal(), jitter_marginal() Nuisance variation is integrated rather than allowed to redefine the class
Estimate a kinetic population fit_bank() Donors are pure/appropriate and independent of scored participants
Cross-fit an in-sample population bank_loo() All adaptive steps exclude the held-out participant
Define a Route II class restrict_bank() Region is prespecified and has adequate mass
Form a class likelihood class_loglik(), background_loglik() Li1L_{i1} and Li0L_{i0} represent the intended states
Fit the covariate gate fit_gate() Design matrix matches the scientific contrast; separation is handled appropriately
Test a gate effect gate_test() Permutation scheme matches exchangeability; penalised statistics are not called likelihood ratios
Visualise diagnostics plot_bank(), plot_responsibility(), plot_gate() Plots are interpreted as diagnostics, not proof of assumptions

Conditions to check before trusting the output

1. State meaning and class construction

Write the biological definition of both states without referring to the fitted result. Route I needs a state-specific reference population. Route II needs a boundary fixed before the outcome-adaptive fit.

2. Observation model

Confirm the measurement scale, residual noise, censoring mechanism, visit times, and any latent timing offset. The residual scale controls how sharply likelihood evidence separates the states; choosing it too small can harden responsibilities artificially.

3. Candidate coverage and positivity

Plot candidate trajectories on a dense grid. Check that observed records are covered, biologically invalid curves are excluded, and fitted weight does not pile up at arbitrary design boundaries.

4. Honesty

The participant being scored must not contribute to the bank, support screen, noise tuning, or any other outcome-adaptive step used for that score. Use a fully independent bank or exact cross-fitting.

5. Purity or region validity

Route I requires the bank to represent the intended state. Route II requires the marginal population to be restricted to an identifiable, prespecified region. Honesty and purity are separate conditions: leave-one-out fitting can be honest while still estimating the wrong mixture.

6. Transportability or exchangeability

For Route I, ask whether donor kinetics within the state apply to the analysis cohort. For Route II, ask whether the other participants are suitable donors for the held-out participant’s marginal kinetic distribution.

7. Stability and region mass

Report effective support, sensitivity to candidate design and residual scale, and, for Route II, the mass of every restricted region in every fold. These are stability diagnostics; because the oracle bank is unknown, they are not verified bounds on oracle error.

8. Gate interpretation and inference

The fitted gate probability fit$pi uses covariates before the participant’s trajectory. The responsibility fit$w combines that prior probability with the class likelihood ratio. The coefficient fit$gamma is a log-odds association with latent-state probability, conditional on the model.

Use permutation inference when the reference distribution of the plug-in statistic is not established. With firth = TRUE, gate_test() reports a penalised-objective difference and a permutation p-value; it is not an ordinary likelihood-ratio test.

A minimum reporting checklist

Report at least:

  • the biological definitions of states 0 and 1;
  • Route I or Route II and why that route is valid;
  • the mechanistic and observation models;
  • candidate bounds, screens, integration grids, and residual scale;
  • the complete honesty/cross-fitting construction;
  • donor purity and transportability, or Route II region definition and mass;
  • effective bank support and sensitivity analyses;
  • responsibility distributions and the fitted gate contrast;
  • the exact permutation procedure and number of permutations; and
  • limitations, especially within-class covariate effects and kinetic mismatch.

Choose the detailed walkthrough

  • Bring your own ODE: custom mechanistic models
  • Route I: independent reference-bank simulation
  • Route II: prespecified-region simulation

Both simulations expose the latent truth, show how each line of code maps to the MBMM hierarchy, and contain executable recovery checks. Passing those examples verifies the implementation in those controlled settings; it does not substitute for checking the scientific conditions above in a new study.
